canonicalExplanation.summary: Every function call gets a **stack frame** holding its parameters, local variables and where to return. A recursive call pushes a new frame on top; frames **unwind** (pop) as base cases return. So recursion **uses memory**: O(depth) frames, even if each frame does tiny work. Deep recursion can hit the limit: Python stops at about 1,000 frames by default (RecursionError), and C, C++ and Java crash with a stack overflow at a depth set by the stack size. When depth grows with n (like walking a long linked list), rewrite the recursion as a **loop**, or use an explicit stack.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A playlist app counts lessons in a linked list recursively: `1 + count(node.next)`. It works for 50 lessons. A learner imports a 5,000-lesson archive and the app crashes with "maximum recursion depth exceeded". A depth-n linked-list recursion uses n frames even though each frame performs constant local work. In this lesson you'll visualize calls and convert a deeply linear recursion to iteration when appropriate.

sections.heading: The model: frames pile up, then unwind
sections.body:
```python
def count_recursive(node):              # O(n) time, O(n) stack space.
    if node is None:
        return 0
    return 1 + count_recursive(node.next)  # this frame waits for the next one.

def count_iterative(node):              # O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
    total = 0
    while node is not None:
        total += 1
        node = node.next
    return total
```

```text
count_recursive(A) for A -> B -> C.
  frame A waits: 1 + count(B).
    frame B waits: 1 + count(C).
      frame C waits: 1 + count(None).
        frame None returns 0.      <- deepest point: 4 frames.
      frame C returns 1.
    frame B returns 2.
  frame A returns 3.
```

| Recursion shape | Stack depth | Safe? |
|---|---|---|
| linear (list, countdown). | n. | risky for large n: prefer a loop. |
| halving (binary search). | log n. | fine. |
| balanced tree. | log n. | fine. |
| skewed tree. | n. | risky: use an explicit stack. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Doesn't Python optimise tail calls?", "answer": "No. Python, Java and most C/C++ builds don't guarantee tail-call optimisation, so even a tail-recursive function keeps its frames. Convert to a loop."}
```

examples.title: The long playlist that crashed the recursion
examples.situation: A depth-n linked-list recursion uses n frames even though each frame performs constant local work.
walkthrough: **Visualise:** for 5,000 lessons, 5,000 frames each wait on the next call before any returns.
**Uses n frames:** the maximum depth is n, so the default Python limit of about 1,000 is exceeded.
**Convert:** count_iterative walks with a loop in O(1) extra space; a test will count a 100,000-node list without error.
examples.result: Imports of any size are counted correctly, and the app no longer crashes on long playlists.

examples.title: The folder scan that overflowed
examples.situation: A backup tool recursively visits folders. On a machine with a folder chain 20,000 levels deep (a symlink loop gone wrong), it crashes.
walkthrough: Recursion depth equals folder depth here.
Use an explicit stack (a list of folders to visit) in a loop.
Also track visited folders so a loop in the links can't repeat forever.
examples.result: The scan handles any depth without a stack overflow and stops on cycles.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Recursive algorithms use no extra space when they allocate no heap objects.
misconceptions.correction: Every active call holds a stack frame, so recursion uses space proportional to its maximum depth. A linear recursion over n items uses O(n) stack even with no heap allocations.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, where did the O(n) space come from?

analogy.example: Recursive calls are like **a stack of sticky notes**, each saying "when you get the answer below, add 1 and pass it up". With 5,000 notes the pile topples. A loop is **one note you keep updating**: "count so far: 3".
usefulFor: remembering one frame per waiting call
loop = one note updated in place
limitations: Notes can be read in any order; frames must unwind top first.
A short pile (log n depth) is perfectly safe.

steps.explanation: Each call pushes a frame and waits for the next.
A depth-n linked-list recursion uses n frames even though each frame performs constant local work.
Frames pop as each call returns its result upward.

trace.textAlternative: Tracing frames for a list count. Step 1, Descend: frames is A, B, C. Each call pushes a frame and waits for the next. Step 2, Deepest: frames is A, B, C, None (4); local work per frame is constant. A depth-n linked-list recursion uses n frames even though each frame performs constant local work. Step 3, Unwind: returns is 0, 1, 2, 3. Frames pop as each call returns its result upward.

remediation.explanation: For any recursion, ask: **What's the longest chain of calls waiting at once?** If it grows with n, and n can be large, turn it into a loop or use an explicit stack.

recap.summary: To visualize calls and convert deep recursion to iteration, remember each active call holds a frame, so stack space equals maximum depth: n for linear recursion, log n for halving. When depth grows with large n, rewrite linear recursion as a loop or use an explicit stack, keeping O(1) or controlled extra space.
